question: A project manager is defining what the monitoring for a demand forecasting model should report each week. The team proposes reporting the average size of the forecast error. The business plans staffing from the forecast and is affected differently by under-forecasting than by over-forecasting. What should the report add?
option_a: The number of forecasts produced during the week, so the error can be put in context
option_b: The direction of the errors alongside their size
option_c: The largest single forecast error observed during the week
option_d: The average error from the previous week, so the trend can be seen
explanation: Where two directions of error have different consequences, a single magnitude conceals which occurred.
explanation_a: Volume gives scale to the reporting period. It does not distinguish the two kinds of error the business experiences differently.
explanation_b: An average magnitude treats a forecast that is too low the same as one that is too high. The business is affected differently by each, so the direction has to be visible.
explanation_c: A worst case is useful for understanding exposure and is worth including. On its own it still does not show which direction the errors ran.
explanation_d: A trend line on the same measure inherits the same limitation in both periods.

question: A model that passed evaluation is ready to go live for all branches at once. The project manager proposes releasing it to a small number of branches first. The team argues that evaluation already showed the model works and that a staged release only delays the benefit. What does the staged release provide that evaluation did not?
option_a: Evidence of how the model behaves within the live process, at limited exposure
option_b: Another measurement on the same held-out evaluation records before wider release
option_c: An opportunity to collect more training records before the model reaches every branch
option_d: Assurance that the model's infrastructure can carry the full production load
explanation: Evaluation measures the model; a staged release measures the model inside the live process around it.
explanation_a: Evaluation scored predictions against held-out records. A staged release exercises the integrations, the handoffs and the people acting on the output, with a small population carrying any problems.
explanation_b: Re-running the original evaluation repeats a measurement already taken on records the model has already been scored against. It exercises none of the live process around the model.
explanation_c: Records gathered during a staged release can be useful later. Gathering them is not the reason to limit exposure at go-live.
explanation_d: Load behaviour at a few branches says little about full volume, so a staged release is weak evidence for capacity. Capacity is tested separately.

question: A project manager asks what should happen when monitoring signals that a live model's performance has fallen below the agreed level. The team says it would investigate and decide at the time. The model supports decisions that continue to be made while any investigation proceeds. What should be agreed in advance?
option_a: The maximum time the investigation is permitted to take before it must conclude
option_b: Which team member will carry out the investigation when the signal is raised
option_c: The level at which the monitoring signal should be set for the model
option_d: What happens to live decisions while the investigation runs, and who decides
explanation: A response agreed before an incident removes the need to negotiate one while decisions continue.
explanation_a: A time limit adds pressure without saying what happens to decisions during the period. It also cannot force a diagnosis to arrive.
explanation_b: Naming an investigator is a useful part of the response plan. It does not settle what happens to the decisions being made meanwhile.
explanation_c: The trigger level is already agreed in the scenario. What is missing is the response once it fires.
explanation_d: Decisions do not pause for an investigation. Agreeing beforehand whether the model keeps serving, falls back or routes to people prevents that being argued while the exposure continues.

question: A project manager is writing the incident procedure for a live model that supports customer-facing decisions. The team has already covered how to diagnose a fault and how to deploy a fix. Which further elements should the procedure define? Select two.
option_a: Which algorithm the replacement model should use if the fault cannot be corrected
option_b: How live decisions are handled while the fault is being investigated
option_c: The budget available for additional infrastructure during the incident
option_d: Who informs the affected users and what they are told
explanation: An incident procedure covers stopping the harm and telling the people affected, not only repairing the system.
explanation_a: Choosing a modelling approach is development work that follows a diagnosis. It does not belong in the immediate response.
explanation_b: Decisions continue throughout an investigation. Deciding beforehand whether the model keeps serving, falls back or routes to people is what limits the exposure.
explanation_c: Spending authority may matter for a capacity incident. It is not a general element of a model incident procedure.
explanation_d: People acting on the output need to know its status. Without a defined route the information reaches them late or not at all.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling
option_e: The format in which the post-incident report should be written
explanation_e: A report template is useful afterwards and contributes nothing during the response.

question: A model has been live for a month and adoption is lower than planned. Production monitoring confirms the model is meeting its agreed performance level. The project manager wants to understand why adoption is low before proposing any change. Which two sources of evidence should be gathered first? Select two.
option_a: Usage data showing where in the process people stop engaging with the output
option_b: The model's accuracy figures over the month since it went live
option_c: Direct accounts from the staff expected to use it
option_d: A comparison with adoption rates reported by other organisations
explanation: Diagnosing low adoption needs both what people are doing and why they are doing it.
explanation_a: The point at which engagement drops narrows the possible causes quickly, and separates people who do not open the output at all from those who open it and disregard it.
explanation_b: The monitoring already confirms the model is meeting its agreed level, so performance is not the open question. A model performing to target can still go unused.
explanation_c: Usage data shows the pattern and not the reason. Only the people doing the work can say what stops them acting on the output.
explanation_d: Another organisation's rate reflects its own process, staff and tool, and cannot explain the pattern here.
option_e: The volume of records the model processed during the month
explanation_e: Processing volume describes the service running, not whether anyone acted on what it produced.

question: A model produces a risk score for each incoming application. During design the team assumed a reviewer would read the score before deciding. In the live process, the score arrives in a queue the reviewer works through after the decision has been recorded. What should the project manager conclude?
option_a: The reviewer should be instructed to revisit decisions where the score later proves high
option_b: The model cannot affect the decisions it was built to support until it is delivered before them
option_c: The score should be recalculated at the moment the reviewer opens the queue item
option_d: The model's accuracy should be improved so that high scores are easier for reviewers to notice
explanation: A prediction delivered after the decision point cannot influence the decision it was built to inform.
explanation_a: Reworking recorded decisions is costly and does not deliver the intended benefit, which was a better decision the first time.
explanation_b: A correct score arriving after the decision is recorded changes nothing. The integration has to place the output at the point where the decision is actually made.
explanation_c: Recalculating does not move the delivery earlier. The score would still arrive after the decision was recorded.
explanation_d: No level of accuracy compensates for arriving too late to inform the decision.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: A model screens applications and a reviewer confirms each decision before it takes effect. After six months the reviewer confirms almost every decision without change, and the time spent per case has fallen steadily. The project manager is told the human check is therefore working well. What should be examined?
option_a: Whether the reviewer is still examining each case or has come to accept the model's output by default
option_b: Whether the reviewer has enough cases each day to maintain familiarity with the process
option_c: Whether the model's accuracy has improved over the six months of operation
option_d: Whether a second reviewer should be added to confirm the first reviewer's decisions
explanation: A review step that approves everything may no longer be exercising independent judgement.
explanation_a: A near-total confirmation rate with falling review time is consistent with genuine agreement and also with the check becoming a formality. Which of the two it is determines whether the control exists.
explanation_b: Volume affects familiarity and is worth knowing. It does not establish whether the cases are being examined.
explanation_c: Improving accuracy would explain fewer corrections and would not show whether the check still functions.
explanation_d: Adding a layer multiplies the cost and can dilute responsibility. It does not diagnose the existing check.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: Three versions of a model have been deployed over a year. The team can identify which version is running now but cannot say which version produced a given past decision, because the outputs were stored without a version marker. A customer queries a decision made eight months ago. What difficulty does this create?
option_a: The current model cannot be used to re-score the customer's case for comparison
option_b: The team cannot establish whether the model has improved over the three versions
option_c: The customer's case will need to be decided again from the beginning
option_d: The decision cannot be traced to the logic that produced it
explanation: A decision cannot be explained after the fact unless the version that produced it is recorded with it.
explanation_a: Re-scoring with the current model is straightforward and would answer a different question, since that version may not be the one that decided.
explanation_b: Comparing versions is a real difficulty here. The pressing issue is explaining one decision to the customer who queried it.
explanation_c: Re-deciding may follow. It does not explain the original decision, which is what was asked.
explanation_d: Explaining the decision requires knowing which model made it. Without the marker, the team can only guess which of three versions was live and what it would have done.

question: A live model's monthly running cost has risen steadily as usage has grown, and now exceeds the saving the business case attributed to it. The model is accurate and well adopted. The project manager is asked what should happen. What is the appropriate response?
option_a: Continue, since the model is accurate and staff have adopted it successfully
option_b: Reduce the model's usage until the running cost falls back within the original saving
option_c: Review whether the cost can be reduced or the benefit increased, and decide on the result
option_d: Recalculate the original business case using the current cost figures
explanation: An operating model has to keep earning its cost, and that balance can change after deployment.
explanation_a: Accuracy and adoption are means to a benefit. Neither justifies an arrangement that now costs more than it returns.
explanation_b: Cutting usage indiscriminately removes benefit alongside cost, and may remove the most valuable uses first.
explanation_c: A model that costs more than it returns is not worth running as configured. Options include cheaper serving, narrowing its use to the cases with most value, or accepting it is no longer viable.
explanation_d: Restating the case documents the position. It does not decide what to do about it.

question: A team reports a single monthly accuracy figure for a model that serves five customer segments of very different sizes. The figure has been stable for six months. The project manager asks whether that stability is sufficient assurance. What is the limitation of the report as it stands?
option_a: A monthly reporting interval is too infrequent to detect a problem in a live model
option_b: Accuracy is the wrong measure to report for a model serving customer segments
option_c: A stable total can hide a decline in one segment offset by others
option_d: Six months is not long enough to establish that a model's performance is stable
explanation: One pooled figure can stay steady while performance moves in opposite directions underneath it.
explanation_a: Reporting frequency is a separate question worth reviewing. A more frequent pooled figure would conceal the same thing.
explanation_b: Accuracy may or may not be the best measure here, but the defect described is the pooling, which would affect any measure reported the same way.
explanation_c: The pooled figure is weighted towards the larger segments. A serious fall in a smaller segment can be absorbed without the reported number moving.
explanation_d: A longer run of the same pooled figure inherits the same blind spot.

question: A model will be released to a group of users while the remaining users continue on the existing process. The team proposes choosing the first group from one region, because that region's manager is enthusiastic about the change. What should the project manager weigh against that convenience?
option_a: Whether the other regions will object to not being included in the first release group
option_b: Whether that region has enough users to complete the release within the planned window
option_c: Whether that region's manager can take responsibility for the model's outputs
option_d: Whether that region's cases represent the conditions the model will meet elsewhere
explanation: A first release group is chosen for what its results will tell you, not for who volunteered.
explanation_a: Managing expectations across regions is a real communication task. It does not affect what the first group's results will tell the project.
explanation_b: Group size affects how quickly evidence accumulates. Representativeness determines whether the evidence means anything.
explanation_c: Accountability for outputs sits with the organisation operating the model, not with whoever hosts the first release.
explanation_d: An enthusiastic group is easier to work with, and a region with atypical cases produces results that do not carry to the rest. The group has to be informative as well as willing.

question: Monitoring shows that the mix of incoming records for a live model has shifted markedly over six weeks, although the model's measured accuracy has not yet moved. The team proposes taking no action until accuracy declines. What is the argument for acting on the input shift before then?
option_a: Outcomes arrive after the decisions are made, so waiting may expose live decisions before any performance effect becomes observable
option_b: An input shift always causes a fall in accuracy, so the decline is certain to follow
option_c: The measured accuracy figure is unreliable whenever the input mix has changed
option_d: Retraining is cheaper to perform before a decline appears than after one
explanation: A shift in inputs can precede a performance effect that outcome data will only reveal later.
explanation_a: The input shift is observable now; any accuracy effect becomes measurable only once outcomes for the new mix are known. Waiting concedes that interval to a change whose consequences are not yet visible.
explanation_b: A model can be insensitive to a shift in fields it depends on weakly, so a decline is a risk rather than a certainty. The case for acting rests on the delay in observing it.
explanation_c: The figure remains a valid measurement of the records it covers. The issue is what it cannot yet cover, not that it is wrong.
explanation_d: Cost may well be similar either way, and the reason to act early is exposure during the delay rather than the price of the work.

question: A model's upstream data feed fails and delivers no records. The model has no defined behaviour for that case and returns its default output for every request. Downstream systems accept the results as normal. The project manager is asked what should have been in place. What is the answer?
option_a: A second data feed that can be used whenever the first one fails
option_b: A behaviour that makes the failure visible rather than returning ordinary-looking output
option_c: An alert sent to the data team whenever the upstream feed stops delivering records
option_d: A larger cache of recent records that the model can fall back on
explanation: A system should fail visibly rather than continue producing output that looks ordinary.
explanation_a: A redundant feed reduces how often the situation arises and is worth considering on cost grounds. If both fail, the silent default behaviour returns.
explanation_b: Silent default output is indistinguishable from real predictions, so the failure propagates unnoticed. Stopping, or marking the output as unavailable, keeps the fault detectable.
explanation_c: Alerting the data team is necessary and addresses the feed. The model would still be serving default output downstream in the meantime.
explanation_d: Serving from a cache substitutes stale predictions for absent ones, which is a decision to take deliberately rather than a default.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling

question: A model's design is agreed and the build is complete. Two weeks before go-live the project manager reviews the transition plan, which covers training on the new screen and the cutover date. Experienced staff point out several case types they handle today for which the new workflow has no route. What should the project manager settle before go-live?
option_a: Proceed as planned and add routes for those case types in a later release
option_b: How those case types will be handled in the live workflow from the cutover
option_c: Extended training, so staff understand that the model does not cover those case types
option_d: An entry in the project risk log, to be reviewed once the model is operating
explanation: A live workflow needs a defined route for every case that will arrive, not only the ones the model handles.
explanation_a: Those cases arrive from the cutover onwards, so deferring the route leaves them unhandled through the period when the transition is most fragile.
explanation_b: The cases will arrive whether or not a route exists. Agreeing where they go, and who handles them, is what allows the workflow to operate from day one.
explanation_c: Knowing the gap exists does not give staff anywhere to send the cases. Awareness is not a route.
explanation_d: A risk entry records the gap without resolving it, and the cases still arrive on the cutover date.

question: A model is scheduled to run overnight and write its results before the business day begins. The upstream extract it depends on sometimes completes late. The team has not defined what the model should do when the extract is unavailable at its scheduled run time. What should be decided in advance?
option_a: Whether the model waits, runs on the previous extract, or produces nothing, and how users are told
option_b: Whether the upstream extract can be guaranteed to complete before the model runs
option_c: Whether the model's scheduled run time can be moved later into the night
option_d: Whether the results from the previous day can be retained for longer in the system
explanation: A dependency that can be late needs a defined behaviour before it is late for the first time.
explanation_a: Each option has a different consequence for the business day. Choosing at the time, under pressure, risks stale results being presented as current with nobody aware.
explanation_b: Such a guarantee is worth pursuing with the upstream owner and cannot be relied on absolutely. A defined behaviour is still needed for the occasions it fails.
explanation_c: A later slot reduces how often the conflict occurs without removing it. The behaviour on failure is still undefined.
explanation_d: Retention decides what remains available. It does not decide what the model does or what users are told.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: Operational staff can override a live model's recommendation. Over the first quarter, overrides are recorded as a simple count with no reason captured. The count is rising. The project manager wants to understand what the rise means. What should be changed in how overrides are handled?
option_a: Require approval from a supervisor before an override can be recorded
option_b: Remove the override facility, since a rising count suggests it is being misused
option_c: Capture the reason for each override, so the pattern behind the rise can be seen
option_d: Compare the override count with the count recorded by a similar organisation
explanation: An override is evidence about the model, but only if the reason for it is captured.
explanation_a: An approval step suppresses overrides rather than explaining them, and may discourage staff from correcting the model at all.
explanation_b: Nothing indicates misuse, and removing the facility would leave staff unable to correct a wrong recommendation.
explanation_c: A rising count is consistent with a degrading model, a shift in cases, or growing confidence among staff in exercising judgement. Without reasons the three are indistinguishable.
explanation_d: Another organisation's rate reflects its own model, cases and staff. It cannot explain the pattern here.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: A model is due to be replaced by a new version built by a different vendor. The project manager asks what happens to the current model's prediction history, its monitoring records and the documentation of its limits. The team plans to decommission the current environment entirely once the new model is live. What should be preserved, and why?
option_a: The training code, so that the previous model can be rebuilt if the new one underperforms
option_b: The monitoring dashboards, so the two models' performance can be compared over time
option_c: The vendor contract for the current model, in case the replacement has to be reversed
option_d: The prediction and monitoring history together with the model's documented limits, since past operation and decisions may still need to be examined
explanation: Records of a retired model's past operation may still be needed to examine or explain earlier decisions.
explanation_a: Keeping the code is reasonable insurance for continuity. It does not preserve the record of what was decided and why.
explanation_b: A dashboard is a view over data. Preserving the underlying records matters, and the dashboard itself does not.
explanation_c: Contract retention is a procurement matter governed by its own rules and unrelated to explaining past decisions.
explanation_d: Decommissioning removes the ability to show what the model decided and how it behaved while operating. Both can be raised long after it stops running, so the records have to outlive the environment.

question: A model operating in production is owned by the team that built it. That team is being disbanded at the end of the quarter and its members reassigned across the organisation. The model will continue to run. The project manager is asked what must be settled before the team disperses. What is the priority?
option_a: Who owns the model in operation once the team no longer exists
option_b: That the team documents how the model was built before its members disperse
option_c: That the model's code is moved into a repository the organisation controls centrally
option_d: That the team's members remain available to answer questions for a handover period
explanation: A model in production needs a named owner for as long as it runs, independent of the team that built it.
explanation_a: Monitoring, incidents, retraining and retirement all need somebody accountable. Without a transfer of ownership the model runs with nobody answering for it.
explanation_b: Documentation supports whoever takes over and is worth capturing. It does not appoint anyone to act on it.
explanation_c: Central storage protects the artefact. It does not make anyone responsible for the running service.
explanation_d: A handover period helps a transfer that has been arranged. It is not a substitute for naming an owner.

question: A project manager is setting up monitoring for a model that has just gone live. The team asks which measures the weekly operational report should carry, beyond confirming that the service is running. Select two.
option_a: The number of records the model scored during the week
option_b: The version of the software library the model was trained with
option_c: Whether the incoming data still resembles the data the model was built on
option_d: The total time the team spent on model-related work during the week
explanation: Operational monitoring covers both what the model receives and what results from what it produces.
explanation_a: Volume describes activity and is useful for capacity planning. It says nothing about whether predictions are sound or useful.
explanation_b: The library version belongs in deployment records. It is fixed between releases and is not a weekly operational measure.
explanation_c: The model was fitted to a particular kind of input. A shift in what arrives is a leading indicator of degraded predictions, and it is visible immediately.
explanation_d: Effort is a project management measure. It does not indicate how the model is behaving in production.
option_e: Whether the outcomes the model was meant to improve are moving as expected
explanation_e: The model was deployed to change a business result. Tracking that result is what shows the deployment is delivering, rather than merely operating.

question: A project manager is assembling the go-live checklist for a model that will support credit decisions. The team has supplied the evaluation results and the deployment scripts. Which further items should the checklist require before the model serves any live decision? Select two.
option_a: A record of the algorithms the team considered before selecting this one
option_b: A defined signal that tells the team the model is not behaving as expected
option_c: Confirmation that the model scores a record faster than the previous manual process
option_d: A schedule for the next model version's development work
explanation: Readiness covers noticing a problem and undoing it, not only the quality of the model itself.
explanation_a: Recording the candidates supports the development history. It has no bearing on whether live decisions can be made safely.
explanation_b: Without an agreed signal, a fault in production is found only when someone notices an odd decision. The signal is what converts a problem into something the team can act on.
explanation_c: Speed against the manual process is a benefit case, not a readiness control. A fast wrong decision is still a wrong decision.
explanation_d: Forward planning is useful for the roadmap. It contributes nothing to whether this release can go live safely.
option_e: A tested route to return to the previous state
explanation_e: A route back has to be exercised before it is needed. An untested rollback discovered during an incident is an assumption, not a control.

question: A team proposes retraining a live model on a fixed monthly schedule, regardless of how it is performing. The project manager asks what the schedule is based on and is told it was chosen because monthly is convenient for the team's release calendar. What should the project manager establish instead?
option_a: Whether the team has capacity to retrain more frequently than once a month
option_b: Whether a monthly cycle matches the retraining cadence used by comparable organisations
option_c: Whether monthly retraining will produce a measurable accuracy gain each time it runs
option_d: How quickly the conditions the model depends on actually change, and what the monitoring shows
explanation: A retraining cadence should follow how quickly the conditions change, not the release calendar.
explanation_a: Capacity constrains what is achievable once the right cadence is known. It does not establish what the right cadence is.
explanation_b: Another organisation's cadence reflects its own rate of change and its own model. It is not evidence about this one.
explanation_c: Requiring a gain every cycle would rule out retraining that correctly leaves a stable model unchanged.
explanation_d: Retraining too rarely leaves the model stale between cycles, and retraining too often spends effort and introduces change for no gain. The rate the underlying conditions move is what sets the interval.

question: A model has been reverted after a fault. The team wants to redeploy the corrected version the same day to recover the lost benefit. The corrected version has been tested against the case that caused the fault. The project manager must decide whether to approve the redeployment. What should weigh most?
option_a: Whether the benefit lost during the outage justifies redeploying on the same day
option_b: Whether the operational users have been informed that a corrected version is coming
option_c: Whether the fix has been tested beyond the single case that failed
option_d: Whether the team has capacity to monitor the redeployment closely for the rest of the day
explanation: A fix verified only against the case that failed has not been shown to be safe for the rest.
explanation_a: Lost benefit creates pressure to move quickly, but that pressure does not establish that the corrected version is safe to redeploy.
explanation_b: Informing users is part of managing the incident and does not bear on whether the fix is sound.
explanation_c: A change that resolves one case can disturb others. Redeploying on the strength of one test risks a second incident on top of the first.
explanation_d: Close monitoring is a sensible condition of any redeployment. It detects a repeat rather than establishing the fix is safe.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling

question: A model's output will be used by a team that works across three shifts. Training has been scheduled as a single session during the day shift, and the recording will be made available to the others. The project manager is asked whether this is adequate. What is the concern?
option_a: A recording will be longer than the time those shifts can spare during their work
option_b: Two shifts get no opportunity to ask questions about their own cases
option_c: The recording may not capture the screen clearly enough for staff to follow
option_d: Staff on other shifts may watch the recording at different times from each other
explanation: Staff who only receive a recording have no way to raise the questions that block adoption.
explanation_a: Duration is the same for every shift and can be managed through scheduling.
explanation_b: A recording conveys the material but gives those shifts no opportunity to raise questions about the cases they encounter.
explanation_c: Recording quality is a production detail that is straightforward to get right.
explanation_d: Staggered viewing is normal and is not in itself a problem.

question: A model recommends stock transfers between warehouses. It went live three months ago and its recommendations have been accurate. A review finds that warehouse staff act on about one recommendation in five, because acting requires a transport booking that must be made two days ahead and the model runs the same morning. What should the project manager address?
option_a: The timing of the model's output against the lead time the resulting action needs
option_b: The accuracy of the recommendations, since staff are evidently not persuaded by them
option_c: The training given to warehouse staff on how to interpret the model's recommendations
option_d: The incentives for warehouse staff to act on the recommendations they receive
explanation: A correct prediction delivers nothing if the process cannot act within the time the action requires.
explanation_a: The recommendation is sound but arrives inside the booking window, so most cannot be acted on. Moving the run earlier, or shortening the booking lead time, is what converts accuracy into benefit.
explanation_b: Accuracy is not in question and the review shows the obstacle is the booking lead time, not scepticism about the recommendations.
explanation_c: Training helps where understanding is the barrier. Here staff understand the recommendation and cannot act on it in time.
explanation_d: Incentives address unwillingness. The constraint described is a scheduling conflict that no incentive resolves.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: An agreed human-oversight requirement for a live model states that operators must be given the basis of each recommendation and the conditions in which the model is known to be weaker. The deployed interface presents a recommendation and a confidence figure, and nothing else. Operators say they cannot tell when to rely on it. What operational gap must be corrected?
option_a: A higher confidence threshold, below which no recommendation is shown to the operator
option_b: The interface does not deliver the basis of recommendations or the known weak conditions the requirement specifies
option_c: Training for operators on how confidence figures are calculated by the model
option_d: A record of how often operators have followed recommendations at each confidence level
explanation: A confidence figure alone does not show what drove a recommendation or where the model is known to be weaker.
explanation_a: Suppressing low-confidence cases leaves the operator with no support on exactly the cases that are hardest.
explanation_b: The requirement was agreed and the deployment does not meet it. Operators receive a number without the factors behind it or the conditions under which it should be doubted, which is what the requirement calls for.
explanation_c: Understanding how the figure is calculated does not reveal which factors drove a particular case, nor where the model is known to be weaker.
explanation_d: Historical follow rates describe operator behaviour. They do not help an operator judge the case in front of them.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: A model has been running for two years. The business process it supported has been redesigned and the decision the model informs is no longer taken. The model continues to run and write its output to a table. The team has left it in place because removing it was never requested. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Leave it running, since it costs little and may be useful if the process changes again
option_b: Stop the model immediately, since the decision it informed is no longer taken
option_c: Plan its retirement, confirming first that nothing still consumes the output
option_d: Repoint the model at the redesigned process so that its output remains useful
explanation: A model with no consumer still carries cost and risk, so retirement is a decision to take deliberately.
explanation_a: A dormant model drifts further from current conditions while nobody monitors it, so reuse later would be unsafe without rebuilding.
explanation_b: Stopping without checking risks breaking a consumer that adopted the output without the team's knowledge.
explanation_c: An unused model consumes compute, holds data and can be picked up by a consumer nobody expects. Retiring it deliberately, after checking for consumers, removes that exposure.
explanation_d: The redesigned process may need something quite different, so this assumes a fit that has not been established.

question: A live model's agreed conditions of use state that it must not be applied to a particular customer segment. A project manager reviewing operations finds no check anywhere in the system that would prevent such a case being scored, and no record of whether any have been. What should be put in place?
option_a: A reminder to operational staff that the model must not be used for that segment
option_b: A periodic audit that samples scored cases to check whether any fall in that segment
option_c: A clause in the model documentation restating the condition more prominently
option_d: A check that enforces the limit, and a record of cases it stops
explanation: A stated limit is a control only when something enforces it and records what happened.
explanation_a: A reminder relies on people remembering and noticing, and leaves no record of what occurred.
explanation_b: Sampling after the fact may detect breaches that have already happened and does not prevent them.
explanation_c: Restating a condition more visibly does not create anything that acts on it.
explanation_d: A condition written in a document constrains nobody. Enforcement prevents the case being scored, and the record shows whether the limit is being approached.

question: A project manager wants the monitoring for a live fraud model to raise an alert when something needs attention. The team proposes alerting whenever the daily fraud rate differs from the previous day. In a trial week this produced alerts on six days out of seven. What is the problem with the proposed rule?
option_a: It compares against the previous day rather than against the same day of the previous week
option_b: It monitors the fraud rate rather than the model's precision and recall
option_c: It produces alerts without saying which team member is responsible for responding
option_d: It fires on ordinary day-to-day variation, creating too many alerts to distinguish meaningful changes
explanation: An alert threshold that reacts to ordinary variation creates noise and can cause meaningful alerts to be overlooked.
explanation_a: Comparing like days removes weekday effects and is a sensible refinement. The rule would still fire on ordinary variation within the comparison.
explanation_b: Monitoring outcome measures alongside the rate would strengthen the picture. The defect described is the threshold, which would behave the same way on any measure.
explanation_c: Assigning an owner is necessary for a response process. It does not stop the alert firing when nothing is wrong.
explanation_d: Daily rates fluctuate for ordinary reasons, so a rule triggered by any difference alerts on nearly every day. Genuine changes then sit among alerts the team has learned to pass over.

question: A pricing model will replace a manual process. The project manager asks what has to be in place before the switch, and the team answers that the model is accurate and the interface is built. The sponsor wants the release approved this week. What should the project manager establish as a condition of going live?
option_a: A commitment that the manual process will be retired on the day the model goes live
option_b: A way to detect that the model is misbehaving and a defined route back
option_c: A signed acceptance from the sponsor that the model met the agreed accuracy level
option_d: A plan to retrain the model on a monthly cycle once it has been operating
explanation: A release is ready when the organisation can detect a problem and return to a known good state.
explanation_a: Retiring the fallback on day one removes the option of reverting. That is the opposite of what a safe release needs.
explanation_b: Accuracy in evaluation does not guarantee correct behaviour in production. Without detection and a way to revert, a fault continues unnoticed and cannot be undone quickly.
explanation_c: Acceptance records agreement on a figure already measured. It does not give the organisation any means of noticing or correcting a problem after release.
explanation_d: A retraining cadence is part of ongoing operation and may be right. It does not address what happens if the model misbehaves in the first week.

question: A model is retrained on recent data and the new version scores better on the latest month's records than the version in production. The team proposes replacing the production model immediately. What should the project manager require before the replacement?
option_a: Confirmation that the new version was trained on more records than the version in production
option_b: A demonstration that the new version scores better on the original evaluation set as well
option_c: The same release controls that applied to the original deployment, including a route back
option_d: Agreement from the sponsor that the improvement justifies the cost of the retraining work
explanation: A replacement model is a new release and carries the same release risks as the first one.
explanation_a: More training records do not by themselves establish that the new version is ready for production.
explanation_b: Scoring well on the older set is a reasonable check to run. It still does not address how the new version behaves once it is making live decisions.
explanation_c: A retrained model is new software making live decisions. A better score on one month does not remove the need for staged exposure, monitoring and the ability to revert.
explanation_d: The retraining work is already done, so its cost is not recoverable and should not shape the release decision.

question: During an incident, the project manager finds that three people are each investigating the same live model fault from different angles, one has restarted a service, and nobody has told the operational users anything. The team is capable and working hard. What does the situation lack?
option_a: A single person coordinating the response and communicating out
option_b: More people assigned to the investigation so that the cause is found sooner
option_c: A rule that no service may be restarted during an active incident
option_d: A technical tool that shows the state of every service in one place
explanation: An incident needs someone coordinating the response, not more people working on it.
explanation_a: Effort is not the constraint. Without coordination, actions overlap or conflict, changes are made unrecorded, and the people affected are left without information.
explanation_b: Adding investigators to an uncoordinated response increases the overlap already occurring.
explanation_c: A blanket prohibition would block a legitimate remedy. The problem is that the restart was uncoordinated and unrecorded.
explanation_d: Shared visibility helps a coordinated response and does not create one on its own.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling

question: A project manager plans the communication for a model that will change how a team works. The draft explains what the model does and when it goes live. A colleague notes that staff have asked repeatedly whether the model will replace their roles, and the draft does not mention it. What should the communication do?
option_a: Postpone the communication until the position on roles has been settled
option_b: Keep the communication factual and handle role questions individually as they arise
option_c: Leave role impacts out until every staffing decision has been finalised
option_d: Address the question about roles directly, with whatever is known and not yet known
explanation: Leaving a major question about people's own roles unanswered can undermine the rest of the communication.
explanation_a: Delay leaves staff to fill the gap themselves in the meantime, and the model still goes live on its date.
explanation_b: Handling the same question one conversation at a time produces inconsistent answers and leaves most people uninformed.
explanation_c: Waiting for complete certainty leaves the question unanswered through the period staff are asking it, and the model goes live regardless.
explanation_d: Silence on the question staff are actually asking is read as an answer. Stating the position, including what has not been decided, is what allows the rest of the message to be heard.

question: A model will be embedded in an existing system that has its own validation rules, some of which reject records the model can score. The team tested the model against a data extract and did not exercise the surrounding system. What risk does this create at go-live?
option_a: The model's predictions will be slower once it runs inside the existing system
option_b: The existing validation rules will need to be removed before the model can operate
option_c: Records the model was tested on may never reach it, and others may reach it in a different form
option_d: The model will need to be retrained on records that satisfy the validation rules
explanation: A model tested in isolation has not been tested against the system that will feed and constrain it.
explanation_a: Additional processing may add latency, which is worth measuring. It is a performance question rather than a correctness one.
explanation_b: Those rules serve the system's own purposes and removing them would be a significant change with its own consequences.
explanation_c: The surrounding rules decide what arrives. Testing against an extract says nothing about what the live system passes through, rejects or transforms on the way.
explanation_d: Retraining may follow if the live input turns out to differ. The immediate risk is that nobody yet knows what the live input looks like.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: A model will make routine decisions automatically and refer borderline cases to a person. The project manager asks how a borderline case is identified. The team says the model will refer cases it is unsure about, but no rule has been written down for what counts as unsure. What should be defined before go-live?
option_a: The number of staff available to review the cases that are referred
option_b: The explicit condition that sends a case to a person
option_c: The average time a reviewer should spend on each referred case
option_d: The order in which referred cases are presented to the reviewer
explanation: A referral rule has to be explicit, or nobody can say which cases a person will actually see.
explanation_a: Staffing follows from knowing the referral volume, which is not yet knowable. The rule has to come first.
explanation_b: Without a written rule, neither the team nor the reviewers can say which cases will arrive, how many there will be, or whether the ones that matter are among them.
explanation_c: A target handling time is an operational standard set once the work is understood. It does not define which cases arrive.
explanation_d: Queue ordering affects which case is seen first. It does not determine what enters the queue.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: A new version of a live model is deployed. Two weeks later the business reports that outcomes have worsened. The team wants to compare the two versions' behaviour over that period but finds that the previous version's predictions were overwritten as each new one was written. What has been lost?
option_a: The record needed to compare the two versions' behaviour before and after the change
option_b: The ability to revert to the previous version of the model
option_c: The training data that the previous version of the model was built on
option_d: The record of which staff acted on the previous version's predictions
explanation: Comparing behaviour across a version change requires that the earlier version's outputs were retained.
explanation_a: Without the earlier predictions there is nothing to set the new ones against. The team can see that outcomes worsened but cannot characterise how the model's behaviour changed.
explanation_b: Reverting depends on retaining the model artefact, which is separate from retaining its predictions.
explanation_c: Training data is stored separately from prediction output and is unaffected by the overwriting described.
explanation_d: User activity is recorded by the operational system rather than by the prediction store.

question: A model that affects customers has been live for a year. The organisation's governance body asks for evidence that it has operated within its agreed conditions of use throughout that period. The team can produce the original evaluation report and a monitoring dashboard that displays only current values; historical monitoring records were not retained. What is inadequate about that evidence?
option_a: The evaluation report will have been superseded by later versions of the model
option_b: The dashboard shows technical measures rather than the conditions of use
option_c: The governance body should have specified the evidence it required at the outset
option_d: Neither shows how the model behaved across the year in between
explanation: Assurance over a period needs a record from across that period, not the current state and the starting point.
explanation_a: The report describes the model before release, and whether it was superseded is a separate matter. The gap is the absence of any record spanning the year.
explanation_b: A dashboard can carry measures tied to the agreed conditions. What it cannot do is show the past.
explanation_c: Specifying evidence upfront would have helped and does not change what can be produced now.
explanation_d: The evaluation describes the model before release and the dashboard describes it now. Nothing evidences the months between, which is the period the governance body asked about.

question: A model has been live for two months. The project manager asks who reviews the monitoring output and learns that the dashboard exists but nobody has a standing responsibility to look at it. The team says the dashboard is available to everyone who needs it. What should the project manager conclude?
option_a: The dashboard should be replaced by automated alerts so that nobody needs to review it
option_b: Availability is not oversight, so a named owner and a review cadence are needed
option_c: Access to the dashboard should be restricted to the team that built the model
option_d: Two months of operation without review is acceptable while the model is still new
explanation: Monitoring that nobody is accountable for reviewing is a record, not a control.
explanation_a: Alerts cover the conditions someone anticipated. Periodic review is what catches the gradual changes no alert was written for, so alerts supplement review rather than replace it.
explanation_b: A dashboard open to everyone is watched by no one in particular. Detection depends on somebody being responsible for looking, on a known schedule, and for acting on what they see.
explanation_c: Narrowing access does not create responsibility, and it may remove the operational users best placed to notice a problem.
explanation_d: Leaving monitoring unread is not justified merely because the model is new. The monitoring exists so that emerging behaviour can be detected and acted on.

question: A team plans to route a small share of live traffic to a new model while the existing model continues to serve the rest, comparing outcomes before deciding whether to switch fully. A stakeholder asks why the new model is not simply evaluated on recent historical data instead. What does the live comparison add?
option_a: The new model can be trained further on the traffic it receives during the comparison
option_b: A live comparison needs a smaller sample than a historical evaluation to reach a conclusion
option_c: Both models face the same current conditions, including effects the historical data cannot show
option_d: Historical data cannot be used to compare two models at all once one is already serving traffic
explanation: A comparison on live traffic tests the model against conditions no historical extract can reproduce.
explanation_a: Training on traffic during a comparison would change the thing being compared partway through. That undermines the comparison rather than adding to it.
explanation_b: The sample needed follows from the size of the difference being detected, not from whether the data is live or historical.
explanation_c: Live traffic carries today's mix of cases, current upstream data and the behaviour of the people acting on output. A historical extract reflects the period it came from and none of those effects.
explanation_d: Historical data can compare models perfectly well. The point is what it cannot capture, not that it is unusable.

question: A model that performed well during development has been scored monthly since going live. Its accuracy has declined steadily over eight months, although the code has not changed and no errors have been reported in the data pipeline. What explanation should the team investigate first?
option_a: The model is gradually forgetting what it learned during its original training process
option_b: The test set used during development must have been unrepresentative of the population
option_c: The conditions the model was trained on have shifted away from current conditions
option_d: Accuracy naturally declines as a model scores a larger cumulative number of records
explanation: A steady decline after release points first to the conditions the model was trained on having moved.
explanation_a: A deployed model does not change unless it is retrained. Its parameters are fixed, so there is nothing to forget.
explanation_b: An unrepresentative test set would tend to show a gap from the outset rather than a decline accumulating over eight months, so it fits the observed pattern less well.
explanation_c: A steady decline while the code is unchanged is consistent with conditions moving away from those the model was trained on. That is the hypothesis the pattern supports and the one to test first.
explanation_d: Volume alone does not degrade performance. The measure would stay level if conditions held steady.

question: After a model fault is found, the team reverts to the previous model version within the hour. The project manager asks about the decisions already made on the faulty output during the six hours it was live. The team considers the incident closed because the service is restored. What remains outstanding?
option_a: Identifying and remedying the decisions taken on the faulty output
option_b: Confirming that the reverted version is the same one that ran before the fault
option_c: Establishing why the monitoring took six hours to surface the fault
option_d: Documenting the incident in the project's risk register for future reference
explanation: Restoring the service does not undo the decisions the fault produced while it was live.
explanation_a: Reverting stops new bad decisions. The ones already made stand, affecting real cases, until they are found and put right.
explanation_b: Verifying what was restored is a sound step and quickly done. It does not address the decisions taken during the six hours.
explanation_c: That review should happen and will improve detection next time. It is a lesson for the future, not the outstanding harm.
explanation_d: A register entry records that the event occurred. It leaves the affected decisions untouched.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling

question: A model went live three months ago and is technically sound. Monitoring shows its recommendations are accurate. Usage data shows that most staff in the affected team continue to work as they did before, consulting the model rarely. The project manager is asked whether the deployment was successful. What should the answer rest on?
option_a: Whether the intended change in how the work is done has happened
option_b: Whether the model met the accuracy level agreed before it was deployed
option_c: Whether the model has been available without interruption over the three months
option_d: Whether staff report being satisfied with the model in a survey
explanation: Deployment alone does not deliver the intended benefit if the work does not change as planned.
explanation_a: Accuracy and availability describe the model. The benefit was to come from decisions being made differently, and that has not occurred.
explanation_b: The agreed level has been met, and meeting it was a condition of release rather than the purpose of the deployment.
explanation_c: Availability is a service measure that the monitoring already confirms. It says nothing about whether the model is used.
explanation_d: Stated satisfaction can coexist with unchanged behaviour, so it is weaker evidence than what the usage data already shows.

question: A model's output will be written into a downstream system used by three other teams for their own reporting. The project manager asks whether those teams have been told what the new field means and how it should be interpreted. The team replies that the field is self-explanatory. What is the risk?
option_a: The downstream system may not have a column of the correct type to receive the field
option_b: The other teams may object to a new field appearing in a system they rely on
option_c: The field will increase the storage the downstream system requires
option_d: Consuming teams may read the field differently from how it was intended and build on that reading
explanation: A field whose meaning is not documented may be interpreted by its consumers however they see fit.
explanation_a: Schema compatibility is a technical detail settled during integration and easily verified.
explanation_b: Change communication matters for adoption. The consequential risk is misinterpretation, not objection.
explanation_c: Storage impact is a separate technical consideration and does not address the risk that consuming teams misunderstand the field.
explanation_d: A score arriving without a definition invites each team to infer its own meaning. Those readings then spread into reports and decisions that nobody traces back to the model.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: A model will decline low-value claims automatically and refer the rest to an assessor. The project manager asks what happens when a claimant disputes an automatic decline. The team replies that the claimant can resubmit the claim, which will be scored again by the same model. What is wrong with that route?
option_a: The claimant should be required to supply additional evidence before resubmitting the claim
option_b: The model should be retrained to include the disputed claims and their eventual outcomes
option_c: Resubmission sends the dispute through the same automated decision route rather than to an independent review
option_d: Automatic declines should be limited to claims below a lower value than currently planned
explanation: A challenge route has to reach someone able to reconsider the decision, not return to the route that made it.
explanation_a: New evidence could change the input and might help. Placing the burden on the claimant still leaves no route when the decision was wrong on the evidence already given.
explanation_b: Feeding disputes back into training may improve future decisions. It does nothing for the claimant in front of the process now.
explanation_c: A challenge process must provide a route capable of reconsidering the original decision. Sending the same case back through the same automated route does not provide that independent review.
explanation_d: Lowering the threshold reduces how many people are affected without giving any of them a route to challenge.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: An organisation runs four models in production, each deployed by a different team using its own conventions for naming, storage and release. A project manager taking over operations asks for a list of what is running, who owns each model and when each was last updated. No such list exists. What should be established?
option_a: A common set of naming and storage conventions for all four teams to adopt
option_b: A single inventory of deployed models with owner and current version
option_c: A requirement that all four models be redeployed through a single pipeline
option_d: A monthly meeting at which each team reports the state of its models
explanation: Operating several models requires a single record of what exists, who owns it and its current state.
explanation_a: Shared conventions make future work more consistent and take time to converge. They do not tell anyone what is running today.
explanation_b: Without one record, nobody can say what is running or who answers for it. Monitoring, incident response and retirement all depend on that basic list.
explanation_c: Consolidating pipelines is a substantial engineering programme. The immediate gap is knowledge of what exists.
explanation_d: A meeting circulates information periodically and leaves no durable record between sessions.

question: A model was justified by a business case projecting a reduction in processing cost. It has been live for six months and is performing to its accuracy target. Nobody has measured whether processing cost has fallen. The sponsor asks whether the investment paid off. What should the project manager arrange?
option_a: A report of the model's accuracy over the six months, set against its target
option_b: A survey of staff on whether the process feels faster than it did before
option_c: An updated business case reflecting what has been learned since deployment
option_d: Measurement of the processing cost the business case projected
explanation: A model is judged in operation against the outcome it was funded to produce, not its accuracy.
explanation_a: That report is already available and describes the condition rather than the benefit.
explanation_b: Perceptions are a weak substitute for a cost measure that the business case already defined.
explanation_c: Revising the projection is worth doing once the outcome is known. It cannot substitute for measuring it.
explanation_d: Accuracy was the condition for deployment; the reduction in cost was the reason for it. Only the second answers the sponsor's question.

question: A model recommends which maintenance jobs to bring forward. Outcomes become known only when a machine either fails or completes the period without failing, which can take several months. The project manager wants earlier warning that the model's behaviour may be changing. What can be monitored in the meantime?
option_a: The distribution of incoming data and of the model's own predictions
option_b: Nothing meaningful, until enough outcomes have accumulated to measure accuracy
option_c: The number of predictions the model produces each day compared with its design capacity
option_d: The time the model takes to return a recommendation once a request is received
explanation: Where outcomes are slow to arrive, the model's inputs and outputs give early warning before they do.
explanation_a: Both are available immediately. A shift in the inputs the model receives, or in the pattern of what it recommends, is an early signal that something has changed.
explanation_b: Waiting for outcomes leaves months in which a fault would go unnoticed. Input and output behaviour is observable throughout.
explanation_c: Throughput against capacity is an infrastructure measure. Volume can be steady while what the model recommends changes completely.
explanation_d: Response time indicates the service is healthy. It carries no information about whether the recommendations are still appropriate.

question: A team has run a new model alongside the existing process for four weeks without acting on its output, comparing the two sets of decisions. The results match closely. The team proposes switching off the existing process and acting on the model's output from the following week. What should the project manager recognise about that evidence?
option_a: Four weeks is too short a period for a parallel run to produce a reliable comparison
option_b: Running in parallel tested the predictions, not the process of acting on them
option_c: The close match suggests the model has learned to copy the existing process rather than improve on it
option_d: The existing process should be switched off gradually so both can be compared for longer
explanation: A model observed without acting is not yet tested against the consequences of acting on it.
explanation_a: Whether four weeks suffices depends on the volume and variety of cases seen. The more important gap is what a parallel run cannot test at all.
explanation_b: For four weeks nothing downstream depended on the model. Switching over introduces handoffs, exception routes and workload effects that the parallel run did not exercise.
explanation_c: Agreement with a process the model was built to replicate is expected and is not in itself a fault. It says nothing about readiness to operate.
explanation_d: A longer comparison extends the same evidence. It does not begin to test the consequences of acting on the output.

question: A retrained model is ready to replace the live version. The team cannot say which data extract or settings produced the version currently in production, because those were not recorded at the time. What operational risk does the missing provenance create?
option_a: The new model cannot be evaluated until the production model's settings are recovered
option_b: The production model must be assumed to be performing worse than the new version
option_c: The current production version cannot be reliably reconstructed or traced to the data and settings that produced it
option_d: The replacement should proceed, since the new version's provenance is fully documented
explanation: Missing production provenance prevents reliable reconstruction and weakens both rollback and auditability.
explanation_a: The new model can be evaluated on its own merits straight away. The gap concerns the version already running, not the candidate.
explanation_b: No such assumption follows. The production model's performance is being measured by monitoring regardless of how it was built.
explanation_c: If the replacement has to be withdrawn, the organisation cannot rebuild what it was running before. The same gap leaves the decisions the current version produced without a traceable basis.
explanation_d: Proceeding leaves the organisation unable to return to a version it can no longer reconstruct.

question: A rollback plan for a live model exists as a written procedure. It has never been carried out. The project manager asks the team to walk through it and finds that one step depends on a stored copy of the previous model that nobody has confirmed still exists. What does this show about the plan?
option_a: It needs a named owner responsible for carrying it out during an incident
option_b: It should be rewritten to remove the dependency on the stored previous model
option_c: It should be reviewed and approved by the sponsor before the model goes live
option_d: It is an assumption until it has been tested end to end
explanation: A rollback is a control only once it has been exercised; until then it is an assumption.
explanation_a: An owner is necessary for a response and cannot make a missing artefact appear. The procedure would fail for the same reason.
explanation_b: Reverting requires some previous version to return to, so the dependency is inherent rather than removable.
explanation_c: Approval attests that someone read it. Exercising it is what shows it works.
explanation_d: A written procedure can read correctly while depending on something that is missing. Only running it reveals which steps hold.
topic: Incident response, rollback and failure handling

question: Staff who will use a model's output have been told it is accurate and have been shown how to open the screen it appears on. Several weeks after release they continue to rely on their own judgement. Asked why, they say they do not know what the score is based on or when it is likely to be wrong. What was missing from the preparation?
option_a: A demonstration of the screen given by someone from the team that built the model
option_b: An explanation of what drives the score and where the model is unreliable
option_c: A written procedure requiring staff to consult the score before deciding
option_d: A published accuracy figure so staff can see how often the model is correct overall
explanation: Using a model's output requires knowing what it rests on and where it is weak, not only how to find it.
explanation_a: Who delivers a screen walkthrough does not change that it covers navigation rather than interpretation.
explanation_b: Being told a number is accurate gives no basis for judging any particular case. Staff need to know what the score responds to and the conditions under which it has been shown to struggle.
explanation_c: Mandating consultation can produce compliance without judgement, and staff would still not know when to doubt the score.
explanation_d: An overall rate helps calibrate general trust. It does not help with the case in front of them.

question: A model is deployed into a process that previously relied on a manual step. That step also handled exceptions, which staff resolved using judgement and local knowledge. The deployment plan removes the step entirely. What should the project manager confirm before the change?
option_a: Whether the model can be trained to resolve the exceptions as well as the routine cases
option_b: Whether the staff who performed the manual step will be reassigned to other work
option_c: Where the exceptions the manual step absorbed will be handled once it is gone
option_d: Whether the manual step was documented well enough to reconstruct it later
explanation: Automating a step removes whatever else that step quietly did, including handling the exceptions.
explanation_a: Even if some exceptions could be automated, the stem does not establish that the model handles them. A route is still needed for the exceptions the model does not resolve.
explanation_b: Redeployment is a genuine change management task. It does not settle where the exception cases go.
explanation_c: The manual step did more than the task it was named for. Removing it without a route for the exceptions leaves those cases with nowhere to go once the model cannot resolve them.
explanation_d: Documentation would help a future rebuild. The immediate need is a destination for exceptions from day one.
topic: Integration with business processes and systems

question: A live model produces a recommendation that an operator believes is clearly wrong and potentially harmful. There is an override facility. The project manager asks what happens to that case after the override, and the team confirms the override is recorded but is not routed anywhere. What is missing from the arrangement?
option_a: A route that brings serious cases to the attention of those who can investigate the model
option_b: A requirement that operators justify each override in writing before it takes effect
option_c: An automatic suspension of the model whenever an operator records an override
option_d: A limit on how many overrides an individual operator may record in a period
explanation: An override corrects one case; an escalation route lets the organisation learn the model has a problem.
explanation_a: The override protects the individual case and stops there. Without escalation, a recurring fault is corrected repeatedly at the front line while the underlying cause goes undiagnosed.
explanation_b: A written justification is useful evidence and adds delay at the moment of the decision. It still leaves the record unrouted.
explanation_c: Automatic suspension after any single override would treat one disputed case as evidence of a systemic fault.
explanation_d: A cap would discourage correction of genuinely wrong recommendations, which is the opposite of what the facility is for.
topic: Human oversight and escalation in operation

question: A model in production is updated by the team editing the running configuration directly when a change is needed. The project manager asks how a change made last month could be identified and reversed. The team says the change would have to be recalled from memory. What should be introduced?
option_a: A rule that only one named engineer may edit the running configuration
option_b: A recorded, reversible change process for the production model
option_c: A weekly summary from the team describing any changes made that week
option_d: A requirement to notify the project manager before any configuration change
explanation: A production change that is not recorded cannot be reviewed or reversed.
explanation_a: Restricting who may change it narrows the field of people to ask and still leaves the change itself unrecorded.
explanation_b: A change nobody can identify cannot be undone or examined after an incident. Recording what changed, when and by whom is what makes a production system controllable.
explanation_c: A weekly recollection is incomplete by the same means as the current arrangement, and arrives too late to be reversed quickly.
explanation_d: Notification tells one person a change is coming. It creates no durable record of what was done.

question: A model has operated for two years within the same agreed conditions of use. Over that period the organisation has entered a new market, and the model is now scoring cases from it. No decision was taken to extend the model's scope; the new cases simply arrived through the existing process. What does this illustrate?
option_a: The model should be retrained to include cases from the new market
option_b: The process that routes cases to the model was configured incorrectly
option_c: The agreed conditions of use were written too narrowly at the outset
option_d: Scope can drift without a decision, so conditions of use need periodic review
explanation: Scope can widen through ordinary business change without any decision to extend the model.
explanation_a: Retraining assumes the extension is appropriate, which is the question that was never asked.
explanation_b: The process routed cases as it was built to. The gap is that nobody reviewed the model's scope as the business changed.
explanation_c: The conditions described the situation at the time. Their defect is that they were never revisited.
explanation_d: Nobody chose to apply the model to the new market. The business changed around a system whose conditions were set once and not revisited since against what it was actually receiving.

question: A loan model predicts whether an applicant would default on a loan from the organisation. Its declines are monitored by checking whether each declined applicant later defaulted with another lender, treating such a default as confirmation that the decline was correct. Declined applicants receive no loan from the organisation, so their repayment behaviour with it is not observed. What should the project manager recognise?
option_a: How declined applicants would have repaid the organisation's own loans is not observed, so defaults elsewhere cannot fully validate those declines
option_b: Precision is the wrong measure for a loan model and recall should be reported instead
option_c: Checking defaults elsewhere is unreliable because other lenders apply different criteria
option_d: The monitoring should be run weekly rather than at the end of each reporting period
explanation: Acting on a prediction can prevent the outcome that would have shown whether it was right.
explanation_a: Repayment under the organisation's own terms is the outcome the decline was predicting, and the decline itself prevents it being observed. A default recorded with another lender is a different event and only a partial substitute.
explanation_b: A different measure faces the same limitation, since it too depends on outcomes for applicants who were declined. Changing what is reported does not supply the missing observations.
explanation_c: Differences between lenders do add noise to that external signal. The more fundamental issue is that the organisation's own outcome is never observed for declined applicants.
explanation_d: Frequency does not create observations that the decision itself prevented.

question: A model is scheduled to go live on a date fixed in the project plan. Two days before, the team reports that the connection to one upstream source is intermittent and that records sometimes arrive incomplete. The model would still produce an output for those records. What should the project manager do?
option_a: Proceed on the fixed date and record the intermittent connection in the project risk log
option_b: Proceed on the fixed date and correct the upstream connection during the following sprint
option_c: Hold the release until the behaviour on incomplete records is known and acceptable
option_d: Proceed and instruct users to disregard any prediction that appears unreasonable to them
explanation: A release date is a plan, not a reason to put a known defect in front of users.
explanation_a: Logging a risk documents it without addressing it. The release would still put an unexamined behaviour into use.
explanation_b: Scheduling a later fix leaves the intervening period running on incomplete input with unknown consequences.
explanation_c: The model would return output for records that are missing information, and nobody knows whether that output is sound. Going live would put unverified predictions into real decisions.
explanation_d: This transfers the problem to users who have no way to know which predictions were built on incomplete records.

question: A model that predicts delivery delays is retrained automatically each week on the most recent data, with the new version replacing the old one without review. After a period in which a strike disrupted operations, the model began predicting delays far more often. What does this reveal about the arrangement?
option_a: The model should be retrained more frequently so that the strike period is replaced sooner
option_b: Unrepresentative recent conditions were learned and carried into normal operation without anyone checking
option_c: The model should be trained on a longer history so that one week has less influence
option_d: Weekly retraining is too frequent for a model predicting delivery delays
explanation: Automatic retraining can absorb exceptional recent conditions that may not represent subsequent operation.
explanation_a: More frequent retraining would move on from the strike faster and would equally absorb the next exceptional period. The missing control is the review, not the interval.
explanation_b: The strike period is now part of the training data. With no review between retraining and release, an exceptional period is carried forward as the model's expectation of an ordinary week.
